work.title: Adjustment Team
work.later_use: Adapted, much altered, as the 2011 film The Adjustment Bureau.

source.note: Locator into the git-ignored reading corpus. No primary text is stored here.

reading.synopsis: A Clerk arrives to make sure a sleepy dog — the neighborhood's Summoner — barks at exactly 8:15 to bring insurance salesman Ed Fletcher 'A Friend with a Car,' getting him to his office an hour early before Sector T137 is taken offline for a scheduled 'adjustment.' The dog oversleeps by one minute. The wrong summons arrives instead — an actual life insurance salesman, who delays Fletcher until he is late rather than early. Fletcher walks into his sector mid-adjustment: the building and everyone in it are gray, de-energized, crumbling into ash at his touch, and men in white robes with equipment chase him out. He escapes across the sector boundary and the world resumes as normal — except that when he returns that afternoon, everything has been subtly re-made: his coworkers look slightly different, Douglas's office is a different shade, Douglas himself is a younger, healthier man. Fletcher is pulled bodily upward in a phone booth to a celestial administrative chamber, where a tired, mild-eyed Old Man explains: an adjustment team was rearranging the world according to a plan, Fletcher wasn't supposed to witness it, and the changes just made to his workplace will nudge Douglas into buying wilderness land in Canada, which will lead to an archaeological find, which will draw Soviet and Western scientists together, which will very slightly reduce Cold War tension. Fletcher is sent home on his oath of silence — and immediately breaks it under his wife's interrogation, saved from having to confess only by a vacuum-cleaner salesman ringing the doorbell at the right moment.

structure.form: short story in four movements, framed by two doorbell interruptions
movements: The Clerk and the sleeping dog: a single overslept minute as the story's entire hinge.
The wrong summons and the office building crumbling into de-energized ash.
The audience with the Old Man, and the plan explained down to its Cold War payoff.
The return home, the interrogation, and the second doorbell.
structure.point_of_view: opens from the Clerk and the dog's perspective before shifting to Fletcher, so the reader understands the bureaucratic error before Fletcher does, and the story's questions become 'what will he see' rather than 'what happened.'
structure.central_device: A single sixty-second clerical error is the entire plot engine — the story's argument depends on cosmic administration being run on the same margins and mistakes as an insurance office.

characters.name: Ed Fletcher
characters.role: real estate clerk, the 'element' out of phase
characters.note: An ordinary, frightened man whose only real test is not the vision of dissolving reality but his oath of silence to the Old Man, which he breaks within the hour.

characters.name: Ruth Fletcher
characters.note: Insists he go back and face the building precisely because she is certain there is nothing there — and is proven wrong without ever learning it.

characters.name: The Clerk
characters.note: Sweats, checks his pocket watch, and takes the blame upward — the story's least divine and most human character, despite working for God.

characters.name: The Summoner (the dog)
characters.note: An ordinary neighborhood dog whose barks at scheduled times are actually cosmic summonses. Falls asleep at the critical second.

characters.name: The Old Man
characters.note: Tired, mild, ancient, and frank about the scale of the operation ('a staggering job... but it must be done'). Explains a plan that runs through real estate, archaeology and Cold War diplomacy without apologizing for how indirect it is.

settings.name: Sector T137
settings.note: An ordinary city block and office building, de-energized for three hours while an adjustment team reworks it down to its wallpaper and its people's faces.

settings.name: The de-energized building
settings.note: Gray, silent, crumbling to ash at a touch — reality's substrate shown as fragile as a stage set being struck.

settings.name: The Sector Board chamber
settings.note: A celestial administrative office with an infinite glowing map of sectors, and an Old Man who sighs about workload like any overworked manager.

motifs: Administration as the operating metaphor for providence — clerks, schedules, sectors, summons, adjustment teams
Reality's fragility revealed by touch: buildings and people crumbling to ash the instant they are handled during an adjustment
A single missed minute as sufficient cause for a witness to nearly be destroyed
The doorbell as narrative rescue device, opening and closing the story
Subtle re-creation: people and objects remade just enough to be perceptible only to someone who saw the 'before'
reading.significance: The story's real subject, confirmed directly by Dick's own later commentary, is theodicy conducted as office management: God's plan proceeds through Cold War archaeology, adjustment teams and clerical error rather than miracle, and the story treats this as more plausible, not less, than a plan executed flawlessly. Dick returned to this story explicitly when developing his mature cosmology in the Exegesis, using 'Adjustment Team' as his own name for the idea that what looks like glitches or déjà vu in ordinary life might be visible seams in a continual, imperfect divine recreation of the world. The story's comedy — an insurance salesman's ordinary irritations standing in for cosmic stakes — is not incidental to that idea; it is the idea.
reading.closing_note: Fletcher is saved from confessing not by resolve but by a second salesman ringing the bell — the same accident of timing that endangered him in the first place now rescuing him.

distinctive_terms.label: Divine
distinctive_terms.note: The Old Man's plan is explicitly divine administration, not metaphorical.

distinctive_terms.label: Reality
distinctive_terms.note: Ed's own word for what he saw 'split open.'

distinctive_terms.label: Soviet
distinctive_terms.note: Names the Cold War stakes the adjustment is quietly working to reduce.

thematic_links_proposed.basis: reality administered by a tired, mild god-figure through bureaucratic adjustment teams
the world's substrate shown de-energized, gray, and crumbling to ash the instant it is touched during reconstruction
the Cold War itself is a target of the adjustment, nudged toward de-escalation through an engineered chain of unrelated events
Fletcher breaks his oath of silence to the Old Man within hours, saved from the consequence only by accident

pkd_on_this_work.summary: Unusually direct: Dick names this story explicitly as the source image for a piece of his mature cosmology in the Exegesis.

evidence.source: The Exegesis of Philip K. Dick
evidence.quote: I suppose it is possible that these are not dysfunctions, though, but deliberate adjustments, à la "Adjustment Team," in the process of continual creation.
evidence.reading: The clearest statement in the archive: Dick using his own 1954 story as shorthand for a real hypothesis about perceived glitches in reality being visible seams of ongoing divine recreation.

evidence.source: The Exegesis of Philip K. Dick
evidence.quote: hardly an economical or orderly way for God to handle things. (You'll find early stories of mine such as "Adjustment Team" and "The Commuter" dealing with post-screwup changes; they're always bad news to the Creator
evidence.reading: Dick groups this story with 'The Commuter' under one idea — that his fiction had been rehearsing a theology of divine error decades before the Exegesis tried to state it directly.

evidence.source: The Exegesis of Philip K. Dick
evidence.quote: Also, there is to me the real thought that adjustments (à la "Adjustment Team") are being made in our past, which are to an ever increasing degree making a certain "alternate
evidence.reading: Extends the idea from present-tense glitches to retroactive adjustment of the past itself — a theme the sentence is cut off before completing; worth reading in full at the locator.

evidence.author: Christopher Palmer
evidence.quote: The moment of dissolution is often described, always horrifying (even when, as in "Adjustment Team", the purpose behind it is benign — indeed, in that case, divine)
evidence.reading: Palmer's key distinction: the imagery of dissolution recurs across Dick's fiction, but this story is unusual in pairing it with a benevolent cause, which does not make the imagery itself less frightening.

evidence.author: Christopher Palmer
evidence.reading: Palmer notes a recurring animal-perception device across the two stories — dogs positioned as beings who perceive a hidden order humans cannot.

open_questions: The Exegesis passage at line 1735 about adjustments to the past is cut off mid-sentence in the captured window and should be read in full.
The 2011 film adaptation departs sharply from the story (a romance plot replaces the marriage-under-strain plot). Worth a dedicated comparison note if the site ever covers adaptations.
Palmer's dog-perception pairing with 'Roog' is suggestive but stated in a single clause; the surrounding argument should be read for what he thinks it means.
